body.p: On 6 November 2026 HSE published the outcome of the prosecution of Ask Scaffolding Ltd. On 5 July 2023 trainee scaffolder Michael Swales was erecting scaffolding at the front of a two-storey house on a residential development near Ripon in North Yorkshire. He fell five metres after standing on an unsecured scaffolding board. There were inadequate measures to prevent or mitigate the fall. He died at the scene. The company pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 4(1)(c) of the Work at Height Regulations 2005 and was fined £16,000, ordered to pay £8,000 costs and a £2,000 victim surcharge at Leeds Magistrates’ Court on 4 November 2026.

HSE’s investigation found that the scaffolding work on the day was unsafe and did not follow industry guidance. Safe zones had not been established and neither the trainee nor his colleague was using a harness or lanyard. A post-accident inspection identified that guardrails had not been installed where required. Witnesses indicated that scaffolding work was regularly carried out without following the guidance. Scaffold erection, alteration and dismantling are temporary works. Failure to control the incomplete structure places both the scaffolders and anyone below at risk. The principal contractor and the scaffolding contractor share duties to plan, manage and monitor the work under CDM 2015 and the Work at Height Regulations 2005.

ul: Enter scaffold erection, alteration and dismantling on the live Temporary Works Register and confirm the design category and any TG20:21 compliance sheet or bespoke design before work starts.
Require a task-specific method statement that identifies how the scaffolder’s safe zone will be created and maintained at each stage of the incomplete lift.
Where a safe zone cannot be maintained, require personal fall protection (harness and lanyard) with a suitable anchor point and confirm competence in its use.
Do not allow boards to be used as a working platform until they are secured and the required guardrails, intermediate rails and toe boards (or equivalent) are in place for that stage.
Ensure the Temporary Works Supervisor or competent scaffold inspector checks the incomplete scaffold against the method and design before the next lift or before any non-scaffold trade accesses it.

Record inspections in accordance with the Work at Height Regulations and the project procedure; close or update the register entry only after the scaffold is complete or has been dismantled under control.
Escalate any departure from the approved sequence or missing components to the TWC before work continues.

body.p: Build UK published Version 6 of the Common Assessment Standard on 1 November 2026. The Building Safety section (Section 7) now operates on an active opt-out basis. Scaffolding and temporary works are not within the scope of the Building Regulations that regulate ‘building work’, unless they form part of the structure once complete. Companies that do not undertake regulated building work must opt out of Section 7 and provide a statement confirming that they do not carry out work covered by the Building Regulations. Competence-related questions previously located in Section 7 have been moved to the Quality section (Section 5) so that they are completed by all companies. Additional items, including a drugs and alcohol policy and fraud prevention procedures, are now mandatory for every company.

The clarification removes questions that were not applicable to pure temporary works or scaffolding activity and that had created difficulty during pre-qualification. It does not reduce the requirement to demonstrate organisational capability, competence or safety and quality management. Temporary works remain subject to the project temporary works procedure under BS 5975-1:2024 and to the duties in CDM 2015. Pre-qualification evidence and the live control of design, installation, inspection and striking on site are separate. Principal contractors and clients who use the Common Assessment Standard will still expect evidence of competence and controlled temporary works processes.

ul: Confirm with your Recognised Assessment Body whether Version 6 applies to your next certification and prepare the required opt-out statement if you do not undertake building work regulated by the Building Regulations.
Ensure competence evidence that has moved to the Quality section remains current and can be produced on request.
Keep the project temporary works procedure, Temporary Works Register, design briefs, category checks and permits independent of pre-qualification status.
Do not treat an opt-out from Section 7 as a reduction in the need for design, checking or competent supervision of temporary works on site.
Where temporary works later form part of the permanent structure, reassess whether the Building Safety section applies and record the decision.
Update supply-chain and pre-qualification files so that clients and principal contractors can see both the CAS position and the temporary works control arrangements.

posts.title: No design, incomplete load path, ongoing investigation: temporary works control still matters
posts.excerpt: June 2026 HSE fines followed a City of London temporary platform collapse with no design or safe-load calculation. CROSS-UK Report 1539 (May 2026) records propping issued without verifying the existing structure could carry redistributed loads. An HSE investigation continues after the 21 October 2026 Banbury scaffolding and building partial collapse. Temporary wooden platforms that collect concrete debris still need a design and a safe working load.

In June 2026 the Health and Safety Executive reported that two companies were fined after a temporary platform collapsed during floor cutting in the City of London, fracturing a worker’s neck and back. The investigation found no design for the platforms and no calculation of safe loading. The person completing the inspection form was not a competent Temporary Works Coordinator. Verbal instructions to clear debris were not enough without a defined load limit and monitoring.

CROSS-UK Report 1539 (published May 2026) shows a parallel gap in propping. Heavy-duty props were issued for column replacement, but the designer had not checked whether the existing beams and slab could transfer the redistributed loads. Once opened up, the beams and slab were shown to be inadequate in bending and shear. Without further temporary works the building could have partially collapsed.

An ongoing HSE investigation follows the partial collapse of scaffolding and an apartment block under construction in Banbury on 21 October 2026. Two of nine workers were hospitalised. Details of cause remain under enquiry; the practical reminder is that scaffolding and temporary stability systems must stay within the project temporary works procedure.

BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM 2015 require a controlled process: design brief, competent design and check, live register, permit to load, and competent supervision. Temporary structures are not “just timber” or “just props.” They carry foreseeable loads and must have a verified load path from the point of application to a suitable foundation or support.

Identify the temporary condition. Design or confirm a standard solution within its limits. Check it. Permit it. Inspect it. Strike it under control.

body.p: On 15 June 2026 HSE published the outcome of prosecutions against Roots Contractors Limited and Diacutt Limited following a February 2024 incident at Paxton House, City of London. Temporary wooden platforms built to collect concrete cores and debris collapsed onto a drilling operative working below, causing fractures to the neck and back and a brain bleed. HSE found no design for the platforms and no calculation of a safe level of loading. An inspection form was completed by a person who was not a competent Temporary Works Coordinator. Verbal instructions to clear platforms existed, but no safe load was known and clearing was not monitored. Planning, supervision and coordination of the drilling work were also deficient.

CROSS-UK Report 1539, published 14 May 2026, describes temporary works for replacement of a defective reinforced concrete column in a multi-storey block of flats. Heavy-duty props had already been installed and a drawing issued. The props themselves were capable of the required forces, but no evidence was found that the prop designer had checked the existing structure. Opening-up showed that the existing beams and slab were not strong enough to transfer the redistributed loads and would fail in bending and shear. The Reporter designed additional temporary works and a method statement. Without those measures a significant part of the building could have collapsed. The Expert Panel noted the need for a verified load path from the point of application through to a suitable support, and for the temporary works procedure (including TWC and checking) to be applied.

On 21 October 2026 scaffolding and an apartment block under construction partially collapsed in Cherwell Street, Banbury. Nine workers were on site; two were taken to hospital. HSE is investigating. Oxfordshire County Council partially reopened the road on 30 October after safety advice, with further temporary closures expected for crane operations to make the site safe. No confirmed cause has been published; the reminder for contractors is that scaffolding and temporary stability systems remain subject to the project temporary works procedure while the investigation continues.

ul: Treat any temporary platform, crash deck, propping system or scaffold as a temporary works item requiring entry on the live Temporary Works Register.
Issue a design brief that defines foreseeable loads, including debris accumulation, and confirm either a project-specific design or a standard solution used strictly within its stated limits.
When propping or supporting an existing structure, require verification of the full load path, including capacity of beams, slabs, walls and foundations that will receive redistributed loads.
Ensure the person completing inspections or issuing permits is a competent Temporary Works Coordinator or Supervisor under the project procedure.
Do not load, alter or strike temporary works until a formal permit has been issued after the required checks.
Maintain documented supervision and clear communication so that workers are not placed under unauthorised or overloaded temporary structures.
Close the register entry only after verification, acceptance and controlled striking under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: CROSS-UK Report 1613, published on 28 October 2026, records a chartered structural engineer’s report of multiple unauthorised changes during construction of an industrial building extension. Construction had commenced without planning approval, without a Building Regulations application, and without compliance with CDM. After a site inspection the Reporter identified numerous departures from the original design that had been implemented without consultation or design review. A steel grillage platform carrying approximately 5 tonnes of plant had been installed although it was not in the original design brief; the structure was erected before any design verification. The main steel frame had not accounted for the additional plant load. Subsequent checks showed that additional bracing was required to some posts. Other defects included alteration of gable frames to portal frames without review, an undesigned beam supporting a windpost, modified windpost head connections that transferred roof loads, bracing interrupted at a splice (leading to overstressed columns), undesigned column and windpost splices, omission of lower-level bracing for openings, uniform pad foundations with no evidence of design (inadequate for uplift in braced bays), and a retaining wall constructed without prior design.

Additional plant platforms, temporary stability bracing, load-path changes and undesigned connections are temporary works items or design-risk items under BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM 2015. Erecting them before verification places the load path outside the controlled design. The Expert Panel states that the number and extent of the changes are a significant cause for concern and that unauthorised alterations create a risk that safety-critical decisions are made without appropriate technical scrutiny. Where a contractor or others alter a design without obtaining approval from the original designer, they assume responsibility for those changes and the associated risks. Effective management of design changes relies on all dutyholders discharging their responsibilities under CDM 2015, including coordination of design and management of design risk. Seemingly minor changes can have significant implications for structural performance and temporary stability.

ul: Treat any additional plant support platform, grillage, temporary bracing or undesigned connection as a temporary works item requiring entry on the Temporary Works Register.
Issue a design brief before erection. Do not allow the platform or altered framing to be constructed until the design (or confirmed standard solution), category check and permit-to-load are in place.
Confirm that the primary structure has been designed or checked for the additional loads and any change in load path or stability system.
Require formal design-change control: proposed changes must be reviewed and accepted by the responsible designer (or temporary works designer) before implementation.
Where design responsibilities are split, establish clear overall coordination so that the completed structure (permanent plus temporary) functions safely as a whole.
Use site inspections by a competent person (TWC or TWS) to identify departures from the approved design before they become embedded.
Record the residual risks and any remedial works required, and close the temporary works item only after verification and acceptance under the project procedure.

body.p: Build UK has confirmed that Version 6 of the Common Assessment Standard takes effect on 1 November 2026. Scaffolding and temporary works contractors whose activities are not covered by the Building Regulations must actively opt out of Section 7 (Building Safety) and provide a statement confirming they do not undertake work covered by those regulations. The change follows NASC correspondence with MHCLG and subsequent clarification from the Housing Minister to the Building Safety Regulator that scaffolding and temporary works are not generally within the Building Regulations governing building work unless they form part of the completed structure.

CAS is widely used by principal contractors and clients to assess supply-chain organisational capability. The previous ambiguity created practical difficulties for scaffolding contractors completing Section 7 questions that were not relevant to temporary works. The opt-out removes that barrier. Competence-related questions move from Section 7 into the quality section (Section 5) and continue to apply to all companies. Drugs and alcohol policies and fraud prevention procedures become mandatory across the board. Companies will complete the Version 6 question set at their next certification after 1 November 2026.

ul: Treat the CAS opt-out as a prequalification clarification only. It does not alter CDM 2015 duties, BS 5975-1:2024 temporary works procedures, or the project temporary works register.
Confirm in design briefs and appointment letters whether any element of the temporary works will form part of the permanent structure (and therefore fall under Building Regulations).
Continue to require competent temporary works design, category checking (CAT 1/2/3 as determined by the TWC), and formal permits to load, use and strike.
For scaffolding interfaces, maintain TG20 compliance checks, weekly inspections under WAHR Regulation 12 where applicable, and controlled dismantling procedures with exclusion zones.

posts.title: Scaffold dismantling: exclusion zone and controlled lowering failed — a fatal board fall
posts.excerpt: On 22 October 2026, 7 Towers Scaffolding Ltd was fined £20,000 at Laganside Crown Court after pleading guilty to a breach of Article 4(1) of the Health and Safety at Work (Northern Ireland) Order 1978. Samuel Magill, a 60-year-old collection driver, was struck on the head by a 2.4 m metal scaffold board that fell approximately 8 m during dismantling on Lisburn Road, Belfast, on 18 December 2024. He died on 5 February 2025. HSENI found the company had not adequately managed the exclusion zone so that people not directly involved in the dismantling could approach the scaffold. He was struck at the outer edge of the zone next to the pavement. The case underlines that dismantling is a temporary works activity requiring controlled lowering and enforced exclusion of non-essential personnel.

body.p: On 22 October 2026, 7 Towers Scaffolding Ltd was fined £20,000 at Laganside Crown Court after pleading guilty to a single breach of Article 4(1) of the Health and Safety at Work (Northern Ireland) Order 1978. Samuel Magill, aged 60 and employed as a collection driver, was collecting scaffold components from a site on Lisburn Road, Belfast, on 18 December 2024. During dismantling, a metal scaffold board approximately 2.4 m long became dislodged from the upper part of the works, fell around 8 m, and struck him on the head. He was taken to hospital and died on 5 February 2025. He had parked on the pavement outside the site and was struck at the extremity of the exclusion zone adjacent to the pavement.

HSENI found that the company had not sufficiently managed and controlled the exclusion zone during the dismantling phase. Measures were inadequate to prevent people who were not directly involved in the dismantling from approaching the scaffold. Inspector Kevin Campbell described the incident as entirely preventable and emphasised that employers must have robust procedures to ensure equipment and components are lowered to the ground in a controlled method, and that exclusion zones must be clearly identified with measures to prevent unauthorised entry. Scaffold dismantling is temporary works. The load path changes as members are removed; falling objects and people outside the working gang (including collection drivers, site staff and the public) create a high-consequence interface. Standard does not automatically mean low risk.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Treat the dismantling sequence as a temporary works activity requiring design or standard-solution verification under the project temporary works procedure (BS 5975-1:2024 management framework).
Define the method of controlled lowering in the method statement and RAMS. Do not rely on free-fall or uncontrolled release of boards, tubes or fittings.
Set the exclusion zone size and boundaries on the basis of the height of work, the components being handled, and the likelihood of dislodgement. Mark it clearly and enforce it.
Control the interface with collection, delivery or other vehicles. Parking and pedestrian approaches must not place people inside or at the edge of the zone.
Use a permit-to-dismantle / permit-to-strike (or equivalent hold point) that confirms the sequence, exclusion zone, supervision and competence before work starts.
Ensure the TWS or competent supervisor is present and that non-essential personnel are kept clear until the zone is released.
Record the activity on the Temporary Works Register and close it only after the scaffold is fully struck and the area is safe.

body.p: Storm Austen produced an official UK peak gust of 76 mph on 23 October 2026. The Met Office recorded 76 mph at St Mary’s Airport on the Isles of Scilly, 75 mph at the Isle of Portland and Needles Old Battery, and 74 mph at Aberporth. Stronger unofficial readings were reported from some exposed coastal locations. London Construction Magazine used the event to explain why a recorded gust cannot be treated as a direct temporary works design check.

Site teams are frequently asked whether a scaffold, hoarding, temporary roof or falsework is “rated for 70 mph” or similar. Without the design basis that question cannot be answered. Wind design accounts for site location, terrain, altitude, topography, neighbouring buildings, height, exposed area, porosity and the intended duration. An open scaffold, a scaffold with debris netting and a fully sheeted scaffold are not equivalent. Added banners, temporarily removed ties, altered hoarding panels, materials stored on platforms never designed for them, or the loss of shielding from demolition can all change the condition assumed by the original design. BS 5975-2:2024 specifically addresses effects of adjacent tall structures, funnelling and vortex shedding for falsework. The design is only valid for the arrangement that was checked.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Identify temporary works particularly exposed to wind (tall scaffolds, sheeted or netted elevations, temporary roofs, hoardings, façade retention, large formwork and falsework).
Confirm that the temporary works register, approved design, inspection status and the arrangement actually standing on site still describe the same structure.

Verify that ties, bracing, anchors and foundations remain as designed. Any temporary removal of ties or restraint is a design change until the designer or competent person confirms the temporary condition remains acceptable.

Establish whether sheeting, netting, banners or other surfaces have been added or altered since the design was checked. HSE scaffolding guidance is clear that sheeting or debris netting should not be attached without informing those responsible for the design.
Secure loose materials, boards and components that could become wind-borne. Follow any structure-specific or manufacturer operating restrictions.

Before severe wind, apply the project procedure for stopping or restricting work. NASC SG46:24 addresses weather-related risk assessment, stopping and resuming scaffold operations, inspection requirements and securing structures.

After high winds (or other circumstances liable to jeopardise safety), arrange inspection by a competent person appropriate to the type and complexity of the temporary works before normal use resumes. On scaffolding this includes ties, bracing, platforms, sheeting, base plates, sole boards and any evidence of movement or settlement. Heavy rain may also affect ground conditions under foundations even where no damage is obvious above ground.

Where a design assumption has changed, or where damage or partial dismantling leaves the installed arrangement different from the approved design, refer the issue back through the project temporary works procedure rather than resolving it informally on site.

First-generation Eurocodes, including BS EN 1991-1-4 for wind actions, remain the applicable UK standards for buildings and civil engineering works until 30 March 2028 unless a relevant authority or project specification requires otherwise. NASC TG20:21 provides recognised scaffold configurations; TG30:24 addresses operational guidance. NASC SG46:24 addresses adverse and inclement weather. HSE scaffolding guidance requires ties to remain within safe working limits and scaffolds to be checked when substantially altered or adversely affected, including by high winds. On 18 December 2024, while a team was dismantling scaffold on a site on Lisburn Road, Belfast, a metal scaffolding board approximately 2.4 m long became dislodged from the upper part of the structure and fell about 8 m. It struck Samuel Magill, 60, a collection driver employed by the company who had arrived to collect dismantled components. He had parked on the pavement and walked toward the work area. He was struck at the outer edge of the site exclusion zone, next to the pavement. He died in hospital on 5 February 2025.

HSENI found that the company had not sufficiently managed and controlled the exclusion zone around the scaffolding during dismantling, so that people not directly involved in the work could approach. Inspector Kevin Campbell stated the incident was entirely preventable and that employers must ensure robust procedures so equipment and components are lowered to the ground in a controlled method, with clear work instructions communicated to all relevant personnel, and a clear identified exclusion zone with measures to prevent unauthorised persons entering. Scaffold dismantling is a temporary works activity. Falling objects and people entering the drop zone are foreseeable risks under the Work at Height Regulations and CDM 2015. Collection and delivery activity must be planned into the method, not treated as separate.

ul: Every scaffold (including system and tube-and-fitting) is entered on the Temporary Works Register with a named TWC, a design or TG20 compliance sheet, and an assembly, use and dismantling plan that specifically covers striking.
The dismantling plan requires controlled lowering of boards, tubes and fittings (gin wheel, hoist or equivalent). Throwing is not an acceptable method.

A physical exclusion zone is established below the work, clearly signed, and controlled by barriers or marshals so that drivers, other trades, visitors and the public cannot enter. The zone must account for the actual drop path, including items that can bounce or travel beyond the scaffold footprint.

Everyone who will be near the scaffold during dismantling — including collection drivers — is briefed on the zone and the method. A person whose role is to keep others out must not themselves be required to enter the zone.

Ties, bracing and platforms that maintain stability of the remaining scaffold are removed only in the planned sequence. Any departure is treated as a design change until the designer or competent person confirms the temporary condition remains acceptable.
A competent person inspects the scaffold before dismantling starts and the permit-to-dismantle (or equivalent) is issued under the project temporary works procedure.

NASC SG4 addresses the scaffolders’ safe zone during erection and dismantling. HSE HSG150 (Health and safety in construction) addresses exclusion zones and preventing materials falling onto people. posts.title: Banbury partial collapse: a prompt to re-check temporary stability controls
posts.excerpt: On 21 October a building under construction in Banbury partially collapsed with scaffolding. Two workers were hospitalised. HSE is investigating. Cause is not established. The incident is a prompt to re-confirm temporary works controls on sequence, bracing and load path — the same themes that appear in recent CROSS reports.

On 21 October a building under construction on Lower Cherwell Street in Banbury partially collapsed with scaffolding. Nine workers were on site. Two were taken to hospital — one with head and leg injuries, one with severe injuries. HSE is investigating. No cause has been established and none is assumed here.

Incidents like this are a prompt, not a verdict. Structural stability during construction is a temporary-works issue until the permanent structure can stand on its own. Sequence changes, incomplete bracing, unassessed load paths into existing elements, and items treated as “just scaffolding” or “just temporary” sit in the same control space as the CROSS reports that keep appearing.

CROSS-UK Report 1479 (January 2026) is a clear recent example: a late contractor change from lifting beams in pairs to lifting them individually created a lateral-torsional buckling risk under wet concrete that took utilisation over 200% without temporary restraints. The Category II check caught it. Many changes do not.

HSE’s structural stability guidance during alteration, demolition and dismantling is unchanged: temporary supports must be designed, installed and maintained for foreseeable loads, by people competent for the item. BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM 2015 Regulation 19 still require the procedure — design brief, design and check, register, permit and competent inspection — not a verbal “it will be fine”.

Separately, Build UK’s Common Assessment Standard Version 6 (effective 1 November 2026) clarifies that scaffolding and temporary works do not fall within the Building Safety Regulations unless they form part of the completed structure. NASC welcomed the distinction. Competence requirements move, not disappear. The procedural controls under BS 5975 and CDM remain.

This week, for every live item that could affect stability:

- Confirm it is on the Temporary Works Register with a named TWC.
- Ask for the design (or documented standard solution), check category, permit and last competent inspection.
- Treat any sequence change or removal of bracing/props as a design change until the designer confirms otherwise.
- Check the full load path, including existing structure that will take redistributed load.

body.p: On Wednesday 21 October 2026 a partial collapse involving a building under construction and associated scaffolding occurred on Lower Cherwell Street in Banbury, Oxfordshire. The site is the redevelopment of a former car sales premises into 19 apartments. Thames Valley Police stated that nine workers were on site; two sustained injuries and were taken to hospital (one with head and leg injuries, one described as severe). There were no reports of anyone trapped. HSE confirmed it is aware of the incident and an investigation is underway. No cause has been established in the published reports.

body.h: Why this is a temporary works prompt
body.p: Until the permanent structure is self-stable, construction sequence, temporary bracing, propping, scaffolding interfaces and any alteration to the load path are temporary works. HSE guidance on structural stability during alteration, demolition and dismantling states that temporary supports must be designed, installed and maintained to withstand foreseeable loads, and that structures should never be overloaded. Items that affect stability belong on the Temporary Works Register under the project procedure (BS 5975-1:2024).

CROSS-UK Report 1479 (published 13 January 2026) describes a late contractor change on a filler-beam bridge deck. Instead of lifting steel beams in connected pairs, beams were to be lifted individually. This introduced a significant temporary stability risk of lateral-torsional buckling under the weight of wet concrete. Assessment showed utilisation exceeding 200% without rotational restraint and temporary LTB restraints. The Category II checker identified the issue; temporary restraints were required. The report notes that late changes to construction sequence can introduce significant temporary stability risks and that the Temporary Works Coordinator role must ensure clarity of design responsibility at each stage.

Build UK has announced that Version 6 of the Common Assessment Standard takes effect on 1 November 2026. Revisions to the Building Safety section reflect that scaffolding and temporary works no longer fall within the scope of the Building Safety Regulations unless they form part of the completed structure. NASC welcomed the clarification after seeking confirmation from MHCLG. Companies will opt out of the Building Safety section where it does not apply, with a confirming statement. Competence-based questions previously in Section 7 move into the quality section so they remain required. This does not remove the need for competence or for the procedural controls in BS 5975 and CDM 2015.

body.h: What a competent TWC / site team should confirm this week
ul: Every item that can affect structural stability during construction (scaffolding that is load-bearing or tied in a way that affects the permanent structure, temporary bracing, propping, sequence-critical elements) is on the Temporary Works Register with a named Temporary Works Coordinator.
There is a design or documented standard solution, an appropriate design check, a permit-to-load/use and a recent inspection by a person competent for that item.

Any proposed change to sequence, removal of bracing or props, or alteration of loading is treated as a design change and is not implemented until the temporary works designer confirms the temporary condition remains acceptable.
The full load path has been considered, including existing structure that will carry redistributed load (see also CROSS-UK Report 1539).

A protection deck spanning a live public highway, carried on independent scaffold legs and aluminium beams, is temporary works. It is not a traffic-management detail and it is not a temporary fence. The deck must carry its own self-weight, temporary construction loads, wind, and later the grit-blasting and steelwork repair operations above it, while protecting the public below. CDM 2015 requires construction work to be planned, managed and monitored. The Work at Height Regulations 2005 require work at height to be properly planned, appropriately supervised and carried out so far as is reasonably practicable safely. BS 5975-1:2024 is the code of practice for a temporary works procedure. It is not a statute and it does not appoint a person. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. TG20:21 and the scaffold designer’s calculations are manufacturer and industry requirements where they form part of the design. The independent legs, the twin aluminium beams, the board deck, the temporary lighting, the interface with the existing west-side parapet scaffold, and the sequence of erection under a full closure are all items that belong on the temporary works register. A 10-day half-term closure is a control measure that removes public interface during the highest-risk erection phase. It is not itself the design. Standard does not automatically mean low risk. A proprietary aluminium beam with a published capacity is not low risk if the legs have no verified bearing, if the sequence leaves an incomplete span over the carriageway, or if the later height restriction is treated as a traffic sign rather than a temporary-works constraint. body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points

Confirm the design brief states the loads the deck must carry now and later — self-weight, temporary works loads, wind, grit-blasting plant and the public-protection requirement underneath.
Verify the bearing and fixings of the independent scaffold legs on both footpaths. Existing parapet scaffold on the west side is an interface, not a free support.
Treat the twin aluminium beams as a designed span. Do not complete the deck by placing boards across an uncalculated gap.

The full closure is the control that removes pedestrians, cyclists and vehicles during the main erection. The method statement must show that the incomplete structure is stable at every stage, including overnight.
The remaining 30% installed under overnight vehicle closures still needs a permit and an inspection regime. Pedestrian access during those nights is a public interface.
The 4.95 m height restriction is a temporary works consequence. Signage and enforcement are traffic measures; the restriction itself comes from the deck.

body.p: On 9 October 2026 Ground Engineering published an industry view by Vicky Mastoridou CEng MICE, development manager at Groundforce Shorco, on thermal loading and soil response in temporary works. Groundforce had published the same author’s note on 5 October 2026. Neither piece is an investigation report or a prosecution. Both argue that a propped excavation designed against a historical weather average can be asked to work outside that envelope in a hot, dry spell and in the rain that follows. Mastoridou writes that site investigations carried out in winter or spring have often been assumed to remain broadly valid through construction, and that this assumption is now the weak point. She uses clay-rich ground, including London Clay, as the example: prolonged drying can shrink and crack the soil and change stiffness and strength; intense rain can then run down those cracks, with localised softening, swelling and a change in pore-water conditions. She states that lateral earth pressures behind a retaining structure can rise faster than a conventional model expects. On the steel, she states that exposed props, sheet piles and bracing absorb solar radiation, so surface temperature can sit above the air temperature, and that a member restrained by walls, walers and connections cannot expand freely. That restraint is described as extra compressive force in the prop, on top of the earth pressure it was installed to carry. Her article says this can use up resistance that had been calculated under BS EN 1997 partial factors, and that a designer may then specify stronger, larger or denser propping, which reduces clearance in the excavation. She also says load-cell readings need interpretation so a thermal spike is not mistaken for ground movement. Groundforce describes summer 2026 as one of the UK’s hottest on record. That is the supplier’s statement. This briefing does not treat it as a Met Office publication.

A hydraulic prop, a waling frame and a sheet-pile wall are temporary works. Heat does not sit outside that definition because the RAMS already covers drinking water and concrete curing. CDM 2015 requires construction work to be planned, managed and monitored. BS 5975-1:2024 is the code of practice for a temporary works procedure. It is not a statute and it does not appoint a person. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. BS EN 1997 is the geotechnical design framework where the project has adopted it; partial factors and combination rules must be taken from the licensed copy and the project basis of design, not from a magazine article. CIRIA C760 and the proprietary prop manufacturer’s data are industry and manufacturer requirements where they are in the brief. The article is professional opinion from a supplier’s development manager. It is not a design, and it does not publish a measured prop-load increase, a steel temperature or a soil parameter for a named site. Standard does not automatically mean low risk. A proprietary strut with a published capacity is not low risk if the brief omitted temperature, if the ground has cracked and rewetted, or if extra props have closed the plant route. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Put the design temperature range, and the expected duration of hot weather, in the temporary works brief. A prop design that is silent on temperature is incomplete.
Ask the designer how restrained thermal expansion has been combined with earth and water pressure. Do not add that case on site by tightening a prop on a hot afternoon.
Treat a change from the investigation season to a desiccated or rewetted face as a ground change. Review before the next permit, particularly in clay.
If the thermal case needs more props or a heavier section, re-check clearance, plant access and the strike sequence. A safer strut that blocks the excavator is a method change.
Where load cells are fitted, agree who reads them and what a thermal spike looks like against ground movement. Do not slacken or re-pressurise from a single reading.
Inspection after a hot day and after intense rain is a hold point, not a welfare check. Look for loss of contact, seepage at cracks, and a frame that was not loaded yesterday.
Sheet piles, walers and frames in full sun are part of the same load path as the prop. Shading is a control only if it is in the design.
Do not proceed until the arrangement has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: On 29 September 2026 the Civil Engineering Contractors Association called on organisations across the built environment to take part in Stop. Make a Change 2026. The campaign runs throughout October. CECA asks employers, workers, clients and other organisations to pause work so people can take part in sessions on three areas: serious injuries and fatalities, serious work-related health conditions, and mental health. CECA states that the campaign has run every year since 2017, involving hundreds of its members, the wider sector and clients, and reaching tens of thousands of operatives. This year’s programme includes workplace substance misuse, trauma, safe driving, drug driving, mental health, the people–plant interface, and the use of AI and video technology. CECA describes itself as representing more than 300 members across England, Scotland and Wales, delivering around £20 billion of maintenance and improvements to transport and utility networks each year. Andrew Rippington, chair of the CECA Health, Safety and Wellbeing Group, said the campaign is about making a commitment, not only taking a pause, and pointed organisations to free events and resources. The campaign page does not publish a fatality table. The figures below are HSE’s, not CECA’s.

HSE published provisional work-related fatality statistics for 2025/26 on 1 July 2026. The release records 126 workers killed in work-related incidents. Construction accounts for 25 deaths, the largest number of any main industry sector, and agriculture, forestry and fishing for 22. Falls from a height account for 31 worker deaths, around a quarter of the total. Struck by a moving vehicle accounts for 24, struck by a moving object for 21, and trapped by something collapsing or overturning for 18. HSE states that the 2025/26 figures are provisional and will be finalised in July 2027. Excluding the pandemic years, HSE describes 2025/26 as provisionally the lowest annual total recorded. A lower national total is not a site control. For a contractor the relevant point is the kind of accident, not the ranking. A fall from an incomplete floor, a scaffold edge or a tower is temporary works and work at height. A person struck at a platform edge or in a plant exclusion is a working-platform and traffic-management interface. body.p: On 6 October 2026 the Health and Safety Executive reported that Daniel Watton, 50, trading as Inside Out Painters and Decorators Property Maintenance, was sentenced at Warrington Magistrates’ Court after trainee painter Connor Lambert was electrocuted. Lambert, 24, from Market Drayton, died on 29 July 2024 while working at a house in Farndon. HSE’s investigation found that he and a colleague were moving a fully extended ladder at the gable end. During that move the ladder either came into contact with an overhead power line or came close enough for an electrical arc to form. Lambert was killed. His colleague suffered burns to his hands, feet and stomach. HSE found that the work at height had not been properly planned, supervised or carried out safely, that the equipment and methods were unsuitable, and that the risks from the overhead line had not been adequately assessed or controlled. The investigation also identified issues with the training and competence of those doing the work. The original plan used a tower scaffold and ladders to paint the exterior, including an area with a glass canopy. HSE found that approach neither suitable nor safe. In practice the work departed from the plan and ladders were used throughout. That method was approved by Watton and was also unsuitable and unsafe. He pleaded guilty to breaching regulation 4(1) of the Work at Height Regulations 2005. The court imposed 16 weeks’ imprisonment, suspended for 12 months, and ordered him to pay £10,645 in costs. HSE inspector Keeley Eves said work at height and work near overhead power lines are both high-risk activities, and that suitable equipment, a full assessment and trained, supervised workers are required. HSE does not set the sentence.

This was a domestic painting job. The failure mode is the same one that appears on a civils site when a long object is walked under a line: the access method and the electrical interface were never one control. A tower scaffold written into a plan is temporary works equipment. It still has to be suitable for the place it stands, including a glass canopy, and it still has to be erected, altered and used by people who are competent for that configuration. A ladder used instead is a change of method. Approving that change without reassessing the line is how the original plan stops being the control. Work at Height Regulations 2005, regulation 4(1), requires the work to be properly planned, appropriately supervised and carried out in a manner which is so far as is reasonably practicable safe. Electricity at Work Regulations 1989 require electrical systems and work on or near them to be controlled so as to prevent danger. HSE’s GS6 is industry guidance on avoiding danger from overhead power lines, not a statute. CDM 2015 still requires construction work to be planned, managed and monitored where it applies, including on a domestic client project through the contractor duties. BS 5975-1:2024 is the code of practice for a temporary works procedure. It is not a statute and it does not appoint a person. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. A mobile tower is not low risk because it is a standard product. Wind, ground, overhead lines, a canopy and a move of a long conductor all change the consequence. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Treat a tower scaffold, a podium and a ladder used for access as items on the temporary works or access register. A domestic client does not take them off the register.
Before the method is accepted, mark the overhead lines, the exclusion zone and the longest object that will be moved. A fully extended ladder is a long conductor.
Do not approve a departure from a tower to ladders without a new assessment. The original plan is not a permit for the method used on the day.

Where work near a line cannot be avoided, the hierarchy is isolation or diversion by the network operator, then distance and suitable equipment. A goalpost or barrier is a control only if it is in the brief and used.
A tower that cannot be stood clear of the line, or that cannot be erected without the ladder entering the zone, is the wrong equipment for that elevation. Do not force the sheet to fit.
Competence is part of the brief. Training and supervision for the people moving the access equipment belong in the permit, not in a card on the file.
A glass canopy, soft ground or a public footpath is an interface. The tower base and the exclusion both have to be accepted before load.

body.p: NASC’s Safety Report 2026 is based on RIDDOR returns from contractor members for the 2025 calendar year. The President’s welcome records that there were no operative fatalities among NASC contractor members in 2025. The fatalities section repeats that: there were no fatalities to operatives working for NASC contractor members in 2025. Members reported 82 RIDDORs from a combined workforce of 20,168 operatives, employed by 332 contractor members. The accident incident rate was 4.07 per 1,000 operatives and the accident frequency rate was 0.21 per 100,000 hours, which the report states corresponds to about one RIDDOR per 470,000 work hours. Of the 82, 28 were specified injuries and 54 were over-seven-day. Slips and trips on the same level were the most common cause, with 25 accidents. Manual handling was second, with 20. Falls from height of persons were third, with 17. Of the specified injuries, falls from height by persons accounted for eight (29 per cent) and slips and trips on the same level for eight (29 per cent). The report also records one incident involving a member of the public that a member reported to HSE as a RIDDOR. NASC’s review of the information supplied did not consider that it met the RIDDOR criteria, but it is included because it was reported to both HSE and NASC. No incidents involving injuries to third parties were reported. NASC states that HSE construction industry fatality statistics were the highest of all sectors in 2025, with 35 fatal injuries, and notes that NASC reporting runs January to December while HSE reporting runs April to March. Scottish Construction News reported the publication on 6 October 2026, including NASC’s statement that the report coincides with NASC Safety Day. This briefing uses the report’s own figures. It does not treat a membership audit as a project check.

A year with no operative fatality inside a membership scheme is a performance record. It is not evidence that the next scaffold is suitable. Seventeen falls of persons, and eight specified injuries from those falls, sit in the same return as the zero. Slips and trips on the same level were the largest group, which is a platform, access and housekeeping problem as much as a harness problem. On a UK site a scaffold is temporary works: configured to the manufacturer’s instructions or a TG20 compliance sheet, or designed where it is outside that sheet, then checked and permitted under the project temporary works procedure. BS 5975-1:2024 is the code of practice for that procedure. It is not a statute and it does not appoint a person. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. Work at Height Regulations 2005 require the work to be planned, supervised and carried out by competent people, with measures that prevent a fall where that is reasonably practicable. CDM 2015 still requires the work to be planned, managed and monitored. HSE’s scaffolding guidance expects erection, alteration and dismantling by competent people, and inspection before first use, after alteration, after an event that may have affected stability, and at intervals not exceeding seven days. NASC membership, an audit and a safety report do not replace that inspection or the permit to load. Standard does not automatically mean low risk. Public interface, incomplete structure, sheeting, loading and ties into a building that is still being altered can take a common scaffold out of a default low category. Match the elevation to the TG20 sheet or the system design. If height, ties, sheeting, loading or the supporting structure are outside the sheet, it is a designed item.
Do not treat zero fatalities in a membership year as a reason to skip the design brief, the check or the permit to load.
Falls of persons were still 17 of the 82 RIDDORs. Control open edges, incomplete lifts and strike sequence before the harness is treated as the control.
Slips and trips were the largest group. Boarding, traps, access and material on the platform belong in the inspection, not only in a toolbox talk.
A tie into a building that is being stripped, altered or not yet at strength is an interface. Accept the tie only against the structure that is actually there.

body.p: On 29 September 2026 Scaffmag reported that PERI UK is supplying temporary works equipment for the Birmingham Spur Dive-Under, delivered by Balfour Beatty VINCI as part of HS2 Delta Junction, north-east of Birmingham. The structure lets one high-speed line pass beneath another. Its main reinforced concrete walls rise to 11 m. PERI UP Flex modular scaffolding is providing access and support around the high wall sections, and access platforms from that system are being used by teams installing reinforcement to the 11 m walls. Scaffmag records that PERI says its scaffold and formwork designs were coordinated by its engineering teams before arriving on site, to reduce clashes between the temporary works systems. For the wall pours, Balfour Beatty VINCI is using PERI VARIO girder wall formwork, which can be configured with closer spacing between girders, walers and ties for the loads from the taller pours. Concrete pressure sensors have been installed on selected wall pours so the team can monitor loads on the formwork and compare them with the pressures calculated at design stage. The wider package described includes MAXIMO panel formwork for foundation works and BECOSTOP stop ends where reinforcement congestion made conventional timber stop ends difficult. As work moves to the roof slab, PERI SCS brackets can be anchored directly to the completed 11 m walls to create high-level working platforms for reinforcement and to support the formwork at the roof-slab edge. Scaffmag records that this removes the need for the working platform to be supported from ground level and avoids ties passing through the finished concrete. Dan Biggs, senior sales engineer at PERI UK, is quoted on the practical benefit of taking accessories, scaffolding and formwork from one supplier. This briefing does not endorse that equipment. It uses the published arrangement as an interface example.

Access, formwork and a bracket platform fixed to young concrete are three temporary works items that share a face. Treating them as one “scaffold package” is how load gets into the wrong member. An access scaffold to BS EN 12811-1 is there to carry people, materials for the stated duty and the environmental actions in its design. It is not, by that fact, falsework or formwork to BS EN 12812 or the formwork sections of BS 5975. Pour pressure, tie loads and the reaction from a slab-edge form belong in the formwork design. A bracket anchored into the wall transfers that platform load into concrete whose age, strength and anchor capacity have to be in the brief. HSE’s temporary works guidance expects any temporary structure to be designed, installed and maintained for the foreseeable loads, and used only for the purpose for which it was designed. CDM 2015 still requires the work to be planned, managed and monitored. BS 5975-1:2024 is the code of practice for the management procedure. It is not a statute and it does not appoint a person. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. A supplier coordinating its own drawings reduces clash risk. It does not appoint the project Temporary Works Coordinator, and it does not replace the design check or the permit to load. Standard does not automatically mean low risk: an 11 m wall pour, public or railway interface, and a change of support from ground scaffold to wall bracket are all reasons to confirm the category. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Register the access scaffold, the wall formwork and the bracket platform as separate items, with a named interface: who owns the shared face, the ties and the anchors.
Do not let the access scaffold carry formwork, pour pressure or slab-edge reactions unless that load is in its design and check. Duty class on a TG20 or system sheet is not a pour-load design.
Brief wall height, pour rate, concrete temperature, tie layout and the design pressure. Closer girder and tie spacing is a design output, not a site preference on the day.
If pressure sensors are used, state what they are for: comparison with the design pressure, and the action if the reading approaches the limit. A sensor is not a permit.
For brackets anchored to completed walls, hold the platform until the concrete strength, anchor type and edge distance are accepted. Do not load a bracket on concrete that has only been struck.
Changing from a ground-supported platform to a wall-anchored platform is a design change. Strike the old load path only under a permit to dismantle.
Keep the supplier’s coordinated drawings in the brief, and still have them checked under the project procedure. One supplier is not one design.
Do not proceed until the arrangement has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: On 30 September 2026 Coroner Megan Fairweather delivered findings, in chambers, into the death of Andrew Stephen Jones, 37. He died at the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital at 2.19pm on 25 July 2021 from blunt force chest injuries after he was struck by a freestanding aluminium tower scaffold while watching his son play football at Mitchelton Football Club in Brisbane. The tower had been installed in April 2021 as a filming platform for matches. It stood in an open, publicly accessible area between two pitches and was expected to remain for several months. Scaffmag’s report of the findings, which links the coroner’s PDF, records an overall height of about 3.1 m, a working platform just over 2.1 m, a minimum base of 1.28 m and a height-to-base ratio of about 1.6:1. The coroner’s findings record the platform at 2145 mm above ground, on four swivel jacks on timber boards to suit a slight slope, and no outriggers. The inquest heard that this was inside the widely used guidance that a tower with a base greater than 1.2 m could be treated as stable where the working height did not exceed three times the minimum base dimension. The coroner found that relying on that ratio alone did not provide an adequate assessment of wind risk. Senior structural engineer Aaron Poole estimated a critical wind range for toppling of 47 to 54 km/h. Evidence before the inquest placed likely gusts on the day between 41 and 68 km/h. AS/NZS 4576:2020 advises that freestanding tower scaffolds should not be operated or left unattended where wind speeds may exceed 40 km/h. Queensland’s Scaffolding Code referred to “strong winds” without defining the term or giving installers a simple method for deciding when extra controls were required. Mr Poole’s evidence was that outriggers, tie-downs, tube-and-clip restraints and additional dead load could substantially increase stability, could withstand wind above 70 km/h, and would very likely have prevented the incident. Because the working platform was below four metres, erection did not require a Queensland High Risk Work Licence for scaffolding, routine inspections were not required, and there was no requirement for a formal handover certificate. The coroner found there had been no formal plan for ongoing monitoring after installation, and that the circumstances raised issues broader than the actions of any individual.

This is a Queensland coronial finding. It is not UK law, and it does not amend TG20, BS EN 12811-1 or the Work at Height Regulations 2005. The temporary works point travels. A low freestanding tower that satisfies a height-to-base rule of thumb can still be unstable in wind, particularly if it is unclad or sheeted, left unattended, standing for months, or placed where the public can be underneath or beside it. Standard does not automatically mean low risk. Consequence here was a member of the public, not an operative on the platform. On a UK site the same arrangement is a temporary works item: design or configure it, check it against the manufacturer’s instructions and the applicable TG20 compliance sheet, and manage it under the project temporary works procedure. BS 5975-1:2024 is the code of practice for that procedure. It is not a statute and it does not appoint a person. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. HSE’s scaffolding guidance expects scaffolds to be designed, erected, altered and dismantled by competent people, and inspected by a competent person before first use, after alteration, after an event that may have affected stability, and at intervals not exceeding seven days. A weather event is that kind of event. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure. Public interface, duration and wind exposure can take a mobile tower out of a default low category.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Put freestanding and mobile towers on the temporary works register, including towers hired for filming, inspection or short-duration access, and towers left standing between uses.

Do not treat a 3:1 height-to-base ratio as a wind design. Match the configuration to the manufacturer’s instructions and the TG20 sheet. If the sheet does not cover the height, the ties, the sheeting or the location, it is outside the sheet.
Brief wind, exposure, duration and public interface in the design brief. Outriggers, kentledge and ties are design controls, not site improvisation after the forecast arrives.

Set a weather trigger before erection: who checks the forecast, what wind speed stops use, and who has authority to dismantle, tie or exclude. AS/NZS 4576:2020’s 40 km/h figure is Australian guidance, not a UK limit. Use the manufacturer’s limit and the project procedure.
Where the public can reach the tower, exclusion and stability are both required. A tower between pitches, on a pavement or beside a site hoarding is a public-protection item.
Inspect before first use and after wind, alteration or a period left unattended. A tower below a licensing threshold in another jurisdiction is not outside inspection on a UK site.

On 24 September 2026 at Bristol Magistrates’ Court the company pleaded guilty to Regulation 4(1) of the Work at Height Regulations 2005 and was fined £120,000, with costs of £5,247.

After the incident the company installed joists from below and kept people off the first floor. That control belonged in the method first: exclusion, a designed temporary deck or crash deck, or work from a safe level. Floor strip-out sits on the temporary works register. The TWC needs authority to stop access to an incomplete floor.

body.p: On 2 October 2026 the Health and Safety Executive published the sentencing of W G Carter Limited, of 81A Eaton Road, Appleton, Oxfordshire, after carpenter Richard “Felix” Roper died following a fall at Manor Barn House, Nether Westcote, Gloucestershire. On 30 August 2022 he was replacing damaged floor joists on the first floor while other workers removed sections of flooring in the same area. Extensive repairs were under way to rotten joists and floorboards. Large parts of the first-floor structure had been stripped, leaving open gaps between joists. Some joists were missing or had not been secured. He fell from the first floor to the concrete ground floor, sustained severe head injuries, and died in hospital the following day. A joint investigation by HSE and Gloucestershire Police found that the work at height had not been properly planned, appropriately supervised, or carried out safely. Workers, including Mr Roper, could reach areas where flooring and structural supports had been removed, and other workers were still removing floorboards, creating and increasing the fall risk. HSE served a Prohibition Notice stopping further work at height until adequate measures were introduced. On 24 September 2026 at Bristol Magistrates’ Court the company pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 4(1) of the Work at Height Regulations 2005. It was fined £120,000 and ordered to pay costs of £5,247. HSE principal inspector James Lucas said a man lost his life because of the company’s failings, and that appropriate controls could have prevented the death.

A floor that is being opened up is not the permanent structure the operatives walked on at the start of the shift. Removing boards and joists changes the load path, the available standing area and the fall consequence. That is a temporary works condition, whether or not anyone has called it one. Work at Height Regulations 2005 require the work to be properly planned, appropriately supervised and carried out in a manner which is, so far as is reasonably practicable, safe. HSE’s published guidance on falls from height says work must be planned, supervised and carried out by competent people. CDM 2015 still requires construction work to be planned, managed and monitored. HSE’s temporary works guidance says any temporary structure must be designed, installed and maintained to withstand the foreseeable loads on it, and used only for the purpose for which it was designed. On a strip-out, the temporary structure may be a crash deck, a scaffold working platform, a designed temporary deck spanning sound joists, or a decision that nobody stands on the incomplete floor at all. BS 5975-1:2024 is the code of practice for the management procedure. It is not a statute and it does not appoint a person. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. Standard does not automatically mean low risk: a domestic barn conversion became fatal because the fall was onto concrete and the sequence was uncontrolled. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Put floor strip-out, joist replacement and any temporary deck or crash deck on the temporary works register before the first board is lifted.
Do not allow people to work on a floor while other trades are still removing boards or joists in the same area. Sequence the opening, or exclude it.
Treat missing or unsecured joists as a failed working surface. Access needs a designed platform, work from below, or a physical barrier, not a verbal warning.
If a crash deck or temporary deck is the control, brief it, check it and permit it before use. A few loose boards laid back over the opening is not a deck.
Give the Temporary Works Coordinator authority to stop access to an incomplete floor. A domestic or small-works site is not outside the procedure.

After alteration, weather or a change of trade, re-inspect before anyone is allowed back on. The method used after this incident — joists installed from below, first floor closed to access — is the arrangement that should have been in the RAMS first.
Do not proceed until the arrangement has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: UK Construction Week Birmingham ran at the NEC from 29 September to 1 October 2026. On 30 September the published programme included two temporary works sessions. Building Safer Sites: Digitalising Temporary Works ran from 11:30 to 12:15 on the Digitalisation and AI Stage. The session description says temporary works are still too often managed through disconnected documents, emails and paper-based processes, making clear oversight difficult and increasing the risk of errors on site. It says the panel would examine how digital tools can help contractors quality-check temporary works structures, standardise documentation and evidence, improve visibility, and capture, share and manage temporary works information through the project lifecycle. Speakers listed on the programme page were Alistair Ringer (Kier Design), Elliott Wilford (BAM UK and Ireland), Georgios Soldatos (Mace Dragados), Harry Seal (Zutec) and Ray Moloney (Costain). Safety by Design: Raising the Standard for Temporary Works ran from 13:30 to 14:15 on the Building Safety and Occupational Safety Stage. The session description says temporary works remain one of the highest-risk aspects of construction, and that effective planning, coordination and oversight are essential. It says the session would examine design and competency requirements, communication, digital processes and site assurance. Speakers listed were Ash Snaddon (Zealux Access Consulting), Chris Milne (Will Rudd Davidson), Purav Patel (StrucTemp LLP) and Siu Mun Li (Constructing Siu-lutions Ltd). This briefing uses only those published descriptions. It does not report what was said in the room.

A software status, a shared folder or a paper register can all fail in the same way: the item is not on the register, the brief does not match the plant or the sequence, the check has not been done, or the permit has been treated as a formality. Moving the register onto a screen does not remove those duties. BS 5975-1:2024 remains the code of practice for the management procedure for the control of temporary works. It is not a statute, and it does not appoint a person or approve a design. CDM 2015 still requires construction work to be planned, managed and monitored, including work that can affect people other than employees. HSE’s temporary works guidance says any temporary structure must be designed, installed and maintained to withstand any foreseeable loads imposed on it, and used only for the purpose for which it was designed, installed and maintained. HSE describes appointment of a Temporary Works Coordinator, with authority to stop unsatisfactory work, as an effective way of managing that duty. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy of BS 5975-1:2024.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Keep the temporary works register current whether it is digital or paper. A missing item is a missing control, not a software issue.
Do not treat a digital status as a design, an independent check or a permit to load, use or strike.
Match the design brief to the plant, geometry, sequence, ground and interfaces that will actually be used.
Give the Temporary Works Coordinator authority to stop work that is outside the brief, the check or the permit.
Inspect before first use and after alteration, weather or a change of plant. A photograph in a system is not the inspection.

Standard does not automatically mean low risk. Consequence, public interface, ground uncertainty and sequence still set the category. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.
Do not implement a conference description as a project procedure. Read it back into the procedure you already have.

posts.title: A return, a 1.5 m lift and a timber brace are temporary works — match the sheet to the wall
posts.excerpt: NASC’s TG20 ePortal update (4 September 2026), restated in Scaffolding Insider on 30 September, adds 1.5 m lifts and scaffold returns to tube-and-fitting compliance sheets. CROSS-UK Report 1525 (13 May 2026) describes ad hoc timber bracing to masonry with no design. Penang DOSH reported a fatal collapse on 8 September 2026 of a temporary catch platform supporting scaffolding during dismantling. For contractors the control is the same: identify the temporary condition, design or configure it, and inspect it before and during striking.
posts.linkedinReady:
A compliance sheet that does not match the scaffold on the wall is not a compliance sheet. A timber brace leaned against a new masonry wall because “that is how we have always done it” is not a temporary works design.

Two UK publications, and one overseas fatality, land in the same place this week.

On 4 September 2026 NASC added two options to the TG20 ePortal for tube and fitting scaffolds: 1.5 m lift heights, and returns. The September Scaffolding Insider, published on 30 September, flags that update again. A 1.5 m lift is the height many bricklayers actually work to. A return is where the scaffold turns the corner. When a return is selected, the compliance sheet includes an extra page for internal and external returns: how far the scaffold extends, how it is connected, and how it is tied as it goes around the building. The new options currently apply to tube and fitting scaffolds in the TG20 version of the ePortal. If the sheet is still a straight run and the site has built a return, you are outside the sheet. The Temporary Works Coordinator should be checking the sheet against the elevation, not against last month’s template.

CROSS-UK Report 1525, published on 13 May 2026, is the other half of the same wall. The reporter describes ad hoc timber bracing to masonry with no design, no calculation and no oversight, and says principal contractors were not asking the TWC for a temporary works design inside the brickwork package. The Expert Panel is plain: a partially built wall can overturn under wind, impact or ordinary site activity. An improvised brace can add a hazard because nobody has checked how it works. Collapses of masonry walls during construction have historically caused serious injuries and fatalities. BS 5975-1:2024 is the management procedure. CDM 2015 still requires the work to be planned, managed and monitored. HSE’s position has not moved: a temporary structure must be designed, installed and maintained for the foreseeable loads on it, and used only for that purpose.

On 8 September 2026 in Bukit Mertajam, Penang, a worker died while dismantling scaffolding. Penang DOSH said he was on the eighth floor when the temporary catch platform supporting the scaffolding collapsed; he and the scaffold fell, and he suffered severe head injuries and was pronounced dead at the scene. Work was stopped and the scene preserved. This is not a UK prosecution and the investigation is not finished. The control point travels. A catch platform, a fan or a crash deck is temporary works. Dismantling is a design case, not the reverse of erection done from memory.

Monday’s check:
- Put masonry stability and scaffold returns on the temporary works register before the bricklayers arrive.
- Match the TG20 compliance sheet to the lifts and returns that will actually be built. If the geometry is outside the sheet, it needs a design.
- Brief the dismantling sequence. A platform that carried the scaffold on the way up has to be checked for the way down.
- Give the TWC authority to stop informal bracing. A photo of a timber prop is not a permit.

body.p: On 4 September 2026 the National Access and Scaffolding Confederation published an update to TG20 in the ePortal. Users can select 1.5 m lift heights when configuring a tube and fitting scaffold, which NASC notes is particularly relevant to traditional new-build work where bricklayers need a suitable working height. The same update adds returns. When a return is selected, an additional page is included in the compliance sheet for internal and external returns, covering how far the scaffold should extend around the return, connection arrangements, and how the scaffold should be tied as it is returned around the building. NASC states that the new functionality is available in the TG20 version of the ePortal and currently applies to tube and fitting scaffolds. The September 2026 issue of Scaffolding Insider, announced on 30 September 2026, includes that TG20 update alongside the top-line messages from SG25 Access and Egress. The magazine announcement does not replace the compliance sheet: the sheet has to describe the scaffold that will be built.

body.h: CROSS 1525: bracing that was never designed
body.p: CROSS-UK Report 1525, published on 13 May 2026, records a reporter’s concern about ad hoc timber bracing used to support masonry walls without a temporary works design, calculations or oversight. The reporter, who describes a life-changing injury from a masonry wall collapse during construction, says these makeshift systems are often poorly fixed and give a false sense of security. The reporter’s view is that principal contractors are not effectively communicating with Temporary Works Coordinators and are failing to identify or request a temporary works design within bricklayers’ work packages, leaving gaps against BS 5975-1:2024, CDM 2015 and the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. The CROSS Expert Panel agrees that partially completed masonry walls can be vulnerable to overturning from relatively modest loads such as wind, impact or construction activities, and that collapses during construction have historically resulted in serious injuries and fatalities. The Panel notes that an improvised brace may be an attempt to address a known risk, but it may not provide reliable restraint and can introduce additional hazards because the behaviour of the system has not been assessed. The Panel points to BS 5975 as the management procedure and suggests simple best-practice solutions, possibly from the Temporary Works Forum, so that low-rise masonry does not depend on a bespoke design in every case or on an unassessed timber prop.

body.h: A catch platform is temporary works, including on the way down
body.p: On 10 September 2026 the New Straits Times reported a Penang Department of Occupational Safety and Health notification of a fatal accident at about 6.15 pm on 8 September 2026 at a construction site in Bukit Mertajam. DOSH said the worker was believed to have been dismantling scaffolding on the eighth floor when the temporary catch platform supporting the scaffolding structure collapsed. The worker and the scaffolding fell to a lower level; he suffered severe head injuries and was pronounced dead at the scene. Following preliminary investigations, Penang DOSH ordered the relevant work to stop and prohibited interference with the scene. DOSH reminded employers that work at height and scaffolding must be planned and carried out through risk assessment and controls, including safe access and egress and fall protection. This is an overseas notification, not a UK enforcement outcome, and the investigation had not been concluded in the report. It is included because the failed element was a temporary structure supporting scaffolding during dismantling, which is the same class of temporary works a UK contractor would be expected to identify, design or configure, and inspect.

HSE’s temporary works guidance says any temporary structure must be designed, installed and maintained to withstand any foreseeable loads imposed on it, and used only for the purpose for which it was designed, installed and maintained. HSE describes appointment of a Temporary Works Coordinator, with authority to stop unsatisfactory work, as an effective way of managing that duty. On a housing or low-rise site that means the brickwork package and the scaffold package both sit on the register: wall stability while the wall is incomplete, lift height and returns on the compliance sheet, and the catch platform or fan during erection and striking. If the scaffold geometry is inside the TG20 sheet, follow the sheet, including the return page. If it is not, it needs a design. Informal timber bracing should not be accepted as a substitute for either. Educational only. Not for construction. Subject to the project temporary works procedure.

posts.title: A temporary walkway in the carriageway is temporary works — the 2013 Red Book is out for consultation, not out of date on site yet
posts.excerpt: Department for Transport, 21 September 2026: open consultation on updating the Safety at Street Works and Road Works Code of Practice (last issued 2013). Draft text proposes minimum usable footway widths, a 1.0 m restricted width limited to 6 m including carriageway walkways, stronger temporary-walkway standards, cycle-route hierarchy, and hard/soft closure definitions. Consultation closes 14 December 2026. The current 2013 code remains the statutory guidance until a revised code is issued. For contractors this sits with CDM 2015 and BS 5975-1:2024: barriers, ramps, boards and excavations in the highway are on the temporary works register.
